source_text: At contra vide quam adversus te et Manichaeum, cuius te semper ruina convolvit, verus sit nobis conflictus, et de eo celer triumphus. Omnia illa, quae in vituperationem divini operis evomuit, primae statim definitionis aratro circumscribimus; cogimusque ut explicet, quid putet esse peccatum, quod claret nihil esse aliud, quam voluntatem appetentem quod iustitia vetat, et unde liberum est abstinere. Quo constituto, omnes illi oblocutionum rubi, qui concretionem corporum pupugerant, et ut ille ait, eradicitus monstrantur evulsi [n87] . Iam vero affectus timoris et sensus doloris, per quos in naufragia hominum cieri tempestatem putavit, non solum nullius mali coactores, sed cum repagulum bonae voluntatis nacti sunt, adiutores et pervectores iustitiae perdocentur. Quis enim formidaret iudicium, nisi timoris admonitu? Quis paenitentiae gemitibus iuvaretur, nisi doloris et internae aegritudinis expiatu? Quid postremo severitas iudicantis valeret, nisi voluntaria peccata illati cruciatus aerumna puniret? Quorum omnium testimonio apparet, nihil aliud esse peccatum, quam voluntatem liberam despicientem praecepta iustitiae; aliterque non stare iustitiam, quam si illud imputet in peccatum, cuius noverit fuisse liberam cautionem; ac per hoc nulla lege, ea quae naturalia sunt, in culpam posse reputari; nec quemquam suscipere crimen, quod non ipse commiserit, cum vitare possit. Qua potentia Manichaeus et Traducianus consumitur, qui effossis totius intellegentiae oculis, rem voluntatis conatur seminibus admovere.
pass_a_gloss: But on the contrary see how against you and Manichaeus, whose ruin always wraps you, a true conflict is for us, and from it a swift triumph. All those things which he vomited into a blaming of the divine work we immediately circumscribe with the plough of the first definition; and we compel him to explain what he thinks sin is, which is clear is nothing other than a will appetizing what justice forbids, and from which it is free to abstain. Which having been established, all those brambles of contradictions which had pricked the concretion of bodies, and as he says, are shown plucked out from the root. Now indeed the affections of fear and the sense of pain, through which he thought a storm was stirred into the shipwrecks of humans, are thoroughly taught not only co-forcers of no evil, but when they have obtained a bar of a good will, helpers and conveyers of justice. For who would fear judgment, except by the warning of fear? Who would be helped by the groans of repentance, except by the expiation of pain and of internal sickness? Finally what would the severity of the one judging avail, unless the hardship of an inflicted torment punished voluntary sins? By the testimony of all which it appears that sin is nothing other than a free will looking down on the precepts of justice; and that justice does not otherwise stand, than if it imputes into sin that whose free caution it has known; and through this by no law can those things which are natural be credited into fault; nor can anyone take up a charge which he himself has not committed, when he can avoid it. By which power Manichaeus and the Traducian are consumed, who with the eyes of all understanding dug out try to apply a thing of will to seeds.

pass_b_english: See, by contrast, how real our struggle is against you and Mani, whose downfall always entangles you, and how swift our triumph over him. We immediately draw the plow of our first definition around everything he vomited out to defame God’s work. We force him to explain what he thinks sin is. It plainly is nothing other than a will seeking what justice forbids and from which it is free to abstain. Once this is established, all the thornbushes of objection that pricked bodily existence are, as the writer says, shown torn out by the roots. [Literary echo: Cicero, On Ends, Book 2.]

As for the feeling of fear and the sensation of pain, through which he thought a storm arose to shipwreck humans, they are shown not merely to compel no evil, but, when checked by a good will, to assist and carry forward justice. Who would fear judgment without fear’s warning? Who would benefit from repentant groans without the cleansing of pain and inward distress? Finally, what power would a judge’s severity have unless it punished voluntary sins by the suffering of inflicted torment?

All these things testify that sin is nothing other than a free will despising justice’s commands. Justice can stand only by reckoning as sin what it knows could freely have been avoided. Consequently, no law can count natural things as faults, and no one takes on guilt for a crime he did not himself commit while able to avoid it. This argument’s power destroys both Mani and the advocate of inherited sin, who, with all the eyes of understanding gouged out, tries to attach an act of will to reproductive seed.

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.
